video.title: Unfortunately, Sales Really Is This Simple (4 Steps)

summary: Codie Sanchez explains a four-part sales framework: fix mindset (don't sell from your own wallet, sell from confidence not need), fix the message (current state, future state, bridge, with the buyer stating the gap and numbers), fix the proof (named, faced, specific testimonials plus anti-sales), and fix the avatar (find people already in pain, sell oxygen not dessert). She promotes her Boardroom community, an upcoming book and a HubSpot growth kit. Key takeaway: ask questions so the buyer sells themselves, price against the cost of the problem, and target buyers already feeling the pain.

tactics.name: Ask-reframe loop to handle 'too expensive'
steps: When the buyer says it's too expensive, ask what it costs them each month to not solve the problem
Get them to state a number and total it over the delay period
Reframe their own words back and compare to your price
Ask the next question and repeat until they close themselves; don't defend or attack

quote.text: you're going to redo their words into your next words and then ask the question again.
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

tactics.name: Current state / future state / bridge discovery
steps: Ask questions to get the prospect to reveal the current pain: who is involved, where time and money are lost, how much
Get them to say a number; write it down and show it to them
Ask about the future state without pitching
Only then present your product as the bridge, restating their numbers

quote.text: the bridge starts to write itself because you're just restating their own numbers back to them
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

tactics.name: Build specific, named proof
steps: Use testimonials with name, photo and screenshot
Add before/after photos, payment links showing amounts, or video
Turn testimonials into stories with numbers
Link to the customer's real social profile for verification

tactics.name: Use anti-sales and avatar filtering
steps: State openly who should not buy
Target people already in pain with a budget
Score prospects as financially ready, reliable, right fit, energising
Ask whether your offer is oxygen (something breaks if no) or dessert

quote.text: You don't sell anyone anything. You find the people already predisposed to what the thing that you are selling.
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

tactics.name: Replace needy phrases with confident ones
steps: Instead of 'just checking in', offer something valuable and say to let you know if interested
Instead of handing off the work, ask 'Does option A or B work better for you?'
Instead of discounting, show the ROI or offer a more expensive option

warnings.warning: Selling from your own wallet and limited beliefs kills deals before the buyer objects; underpricing leaves the highest-leverage growth move unused.

quote.text: do not sell based on what is in your wallet. You are not rich enough.
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

warnings.warning: Selling dessert to someone with an oxygen-level need elsewhere leads to deals that go cold; nothing is on fire so no budget.

quote.text: Dessert means life goes on fine either way.
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

warnings.warning: Vague, anonymous testimonials with no name or photo count as failed proof.
Deals die from lack of follow-up rather than a bad pitch.

quote.text: deals don't die from a bad pitch. They die from nobody following up.
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

lessons.lesson: Price against the cost of the problem the customer has, not against your own sense of what is affordable.

quote.text: We do not sell price. We sell solutions to problems.
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

lessons.lesson: Small price rises have outsized profit impact, so under-pricing is costly (claim attributed to McKinsey, unverified here).
Get the buyer to articulate the gap and the numbers; self-generated arguments persuade more than being told.

quote.text: people are more persuaded by arguments they generate themselves than by the exact same argument coming from someone else
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

lessons.lesson: Prioritise problems that are urgent and painful (oxygen) because those buyers find budget.
Good proof is specific and verifiable (name, face, numbers, before/after); stack enough that persuasion is unnecessary.
Selecting good customers (able to pay, reliable, fit, energising) matters more than pitch polish.
Consistent follow-up cadence and referral partnerships are a key part of pipeline; most stalled deals are asking/follow-up problems.
Neediness and 'circling back' language leaks a weak mindset; lead the buyer with choices and value instead.

evidence_quality.rationale: Generic sales-framework advice from an experienced operator with few verifiable numbers; the case figures are cited second-hand or promotional, and studies are cited loosely via a low-quality Whisper transcript.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Promotes her Boardroom community, upcoming book 'Own or Be Owned' launch event, and a HubSpot-sponsored growth kit.
